paragraphs.heading: A new way to sense the universe
paragraphs.text: LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, is a large physics experiment built to detect gravitational waves from space. Two big observatories were built in the United States to catch these waves using laser interferometry. Before LIGO, all our knowledge of the universe came from light and other electromagnetic radiation, from high-energy cosmic particles, and from limited trips to nearby bodies such as the Moon and Mars. Two smaller observatories now run as well: Virgo in Italy and KAGRA in Japan.

paragraphs.heading: How fine it measures
paragraphs.text: The two LIGO observatories use mirrors set 4 kilometres (13,000 ft) apart. They can sense a change in length smaller than a ten-thousandth of a proton's charge diameter, across an effective path of 1,120 kilometres (700 mi). Virgo and KAGRA, by comparison, use interferometer arms 3 kilometres (9,800 ft) long.

paragraphs.heading: Early ideas
paragraphs.text: LIGO grew out of efforts to test one part of Einstein's general relativity: the existence of gravitational waves. From the 1960s, Joseph Weber in the United States and Mikhail Gertsenshtein and Vladislav Pustovoit in the Soviet Union worked out basic ideas for laser interferometry. In 1967 MIT's Rainer Weiss wrote up a study of how an interferometer could be used, and in 1968 Kip Thorne began theory work at Caltech on the waves and their sources. In 1980 the US National Science Foundation (NSF) funded an MIT study, which showed that interferometers about 1 km long could be sensitive enough, and the next year Caltech built a 40-metre prototype.

paragraphs.heading: Troubled years
paragraphs.text: The NSF pressed MIT and Caltech to join forces and lead LIGO together. A steering committee of Drever, Kip Thorne and Rainer Weiss was refused funding in 1984 and again in 1985. From 1989 to 1994 the project made little technical or organisational progress, though in 1991 Congress agreed to pay for its first year with $23 million. NSF reviews then turned up management and technical concerns, money was held back, and spending was frozen in 1993. In 1994 Barry Barish of Caltech became director, and the NSF made clear this was LIGO's last chance.

paragraphs.heading: Building and upgrading
paragraphs.text: The first observatories were paid for by the NSF and were conceived, built and run by Caltech and MIT. They gathered data from 2002 to 2010 but found no gravitational waves. An upgrade called Advanced LIGO began in 2008, with major help from research bodies in the United Kingdom, Germany and Australia, and the improved detectors started work in 2015. LIGO is the largest and most ambitious project the NSF has ever funded.

paragraphs.heading: Detections, run by run
paragraphs.text: LIGO watches the sky in stretches called runs, with repairs and upgrades in between. The first run, O1, from September 2015 to January 2016, made the first three detections, all merging black holes. The second, O2, found seven more black hole mergers and the first merger of two neutron stars. The third, O3, was halted in March 2020 because of COVID-19 and saw the first neutron star merging with a black hole. By February 2026, after four runs, LIGO had made 391 detections, and the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics had gone to Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish for their work on it.
